entities.summary:
**Identity & Significance**: The International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (ICD) is the main international standard diagnostic tool for epidemiology, health management, and clinical applications. First published in 1900 by the World Health Organization (WHO) based on the work of Sir Clifford Beers, the first president of the American Psychiatric Association, the ICD has undergone numerous revisions, with the most recent edition (11th edition) released in 2018. The ICD provides a universal language for clinicians, researchers, and policymakers to classify diseases, health problems, and health-related conditions, facilitating global health data analysis, research, and policy-making.

**What Happened**: The ICD has played a crucial role in shaping global health policy, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic, as it provided the standard for case definitions and data collection. The ICD has also influenced the development of various health systems, including the US Medicare and Medicaid systems, and has been used in numerous research studies, including those on the epidemiology of mental health and disease prevalence.

**Legacy & Consequence**: The ICD has had a profound impact on global health, facilitating the collection and analysis of health data, informing health policy, and improving disease diagnosis and treatment. The ICD has also been instrumental in promoting international cooperation in health, as it provides a common language for health professionals worldwide.

The ICD's impact is evident in the widespread adoption of its classifications in various fields, including medicine, public health, and research, as well as its role in shaping global health initiatives, such as the World Health Organization's (WHO) efforts to combat infectious diseases and promote mental health.
